name: Big Bone Lick
subtitle: Boone County / salt lick & fossil beds
history: Big Bone Lick was a mineral spring where Pleistocene mastodons, mammoths, and ground sloths left bones in the mud while seeking salt. Native peoples and later explorers—including Christopher Gist—collected fossils here; Thomas Jefferson later studied specimens from the lick. The site became Big Bone Lick State Historic Site, one of Kentucky’s earliest windows on deep time and a waypoint for salt hunters on the Ohio frontier.

name: Lexington Named
subtitle: Fayette County / McConnell Springs
history: In early June 1775, William McConnell’s surveyors camped on a sinking spring of Elkhorn Creek when word arrived of the April 19 fight at Lexington, Massachusetts. They named the camp for that battle and returned east; permanent settlement waited until 1779, when Robert Patterson’s party built a blockhouse near present Main and Mill. Virginia established the town in 1782—the springs chose the site, the Revolution chose the name.

name: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
subtitle: Lincoln County / St. Asaph near Stanford
history: In 1775 Benjamin Logan left Boone's party and built Logan's Station (St. Asaph) near present-day Stanford—a stockade by Buffalo Spring that held through a roughly thirteen-day siege in May 1777. Logan hauled the wounded Burr Harrison inside under fire, then slipped out at night and walked about 150 miles to the Holston settlements for powder. He later helped write Kentucky's first constitution and settled on Bullskin Creek near Finchville in Shelby County.

name: Shelbyville Founding
subtitle: Shelby County seat / Clear Creek
history: Shelby County was carved from Jefferson County in 1792 and named for first governor Isaac Shelby. That October, at the first county court, Revolutionary veteran William Shannon donated about 50 acres on Clear Creek so the new seat would sit on the Frankfort-to-Falls road. Trustees required hewed-log houses with brick or stone chimneys; by 1800 the town had 262 people. Nearby Squire Boone's Painted Stone Station had been the earlier foothold—Shelbyville won the courthouse.

name: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
subtitle: Western Kentucky / 1818 treaty
history: West of the Tennessee River, Chickasaw hunting grounds stayed off Kentucky's settled map until October 19, 1818. Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby negotiated what became the Jackson Purchase: roughly 13,000 square miles (about 2,369 in Kentucky) for annuities. That treaty filled in the western counties from Ballard through McCracken and closed the last big Indigenous title claim inside the state.

name: Frankfort Founding
subtitle: Franklin County / Frank's Ford capital
history: Before it was the capital, the site was a buffalo-trail ford on the Kentucky River. In 1780 pioneer Stephen Frank was killed in a skirmish there; settlers called the crossing Frank's Ford, which shortened to Frankfort. In 1786 Virginia chartered a town on land promoted by Gen. James Wilkinson. When Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort outbid rivals for the capital, and Gideon Shryock's Greek Revival Old Capitol (1830) finally stuck after earlier buildings burned.

name: Bullitt's Lick
subtitle: Bullitt County / Kentucky's first industry
history: Salt was frontier white gold, and the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the Revolution sat about three miles west of present-day Shepherdsville. Capt. Thomas Bullitt surveyed the Salt River lick in 1773; production started in 1779 as workers boiled brine in rows of iron kettles. Pack trains and flatboats carried the salt across Kentucky, a fort went up in 1780, and a boomtown nicknamed Saltburg grew around the furnaces until cheaper salt arrived around 1830.

name: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
subtitle: Jefferson County / Falls of the Ohio
history: Virginia surveyor-turned-militia leader George Rogers Clark staged at Corn Island in the Falls of the Ohio in 1778, then launched the Illinois Campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes from the British. The settlement he left behind became Louisville, chartered in 1780 and named for France’s Louis XVI. Fort Nelson later rose on the mainland as his western headquarters.

name: Battle of Blue Licks
subtitle: Robertson County / 1782 battlefield
history: On August 19, 1782, about 182 Kentucky militia chasing Captain William Caldwell’s raiders walked into an ambush on a Licking River ridge in today’s Robertson County. Roughly 50 Butler’s Rangers and 200–300 Shawnee, Delaware, and Wyandot warriors fired from ravines and bluffs; Todd, Trigg, and Boone’s son Israel were among the dead. It was the settlers’ bloodiest Revolutionary defeat in Kentucky, months after Yorktown.

name: Great Saltpetre Cave
subtitle: Rockcastle County / War of 1812 powder
history: South of Mount Vernon in Rockcastle County, Great Saltpetre Cave was mined hard for calcium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades cut off imported saltpeter for gunpowder. Dozens of workers (many enslaved) leached cave earth in wooden vats and shipped crystals to powder mills until trade reopened after 1815. The Rockcastle Karst Conservancy keeps the preserve today.

name: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
subtitle: Henderson County / Transylvania Company
history: North Carolina judge Richard Henderson reorganized his investors as the Transylvania Company in early 1775, then bargained at Sycamore Shoals for roughly 20 million acres between the Kentucky, Cumberland, and Ohio rivers. Cherokee headmen signed in mid-March; warrior Dragging Canoe opposed the sale and warned the country would become dark and bloody. Virginia later voided the private purchase but compensated the company with Ohio River acreage that seeded Henderson County.

name: Bardstown Founding
subtitle: Nelson County seat / Beech Fork
history: The Bardstown area was explored in the mid-1770s and briefly called Salem. In 1780 William Bard surveyed a town on a 1,000-acre grant for his brother David and John Cockey Owings and set aside ground for public buildings. Named seat of new Nelson County in 1784, it was chartered by Virginia as Baird’s Town in 1788 and settled into the name Bardstown—one of Kentucky’s oldest inland towns.

name: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
subtitle: Jefferson County / Beargrass Creek
history: Virginia surveyor John Floyd led a 1774 Fincastle party into Kentucky, staked 2,000 acres on Beargrass Creek, and came back in 1779 to stockade Floyd's Station near today's St. Matthews. Virginia made him a Louisville trustee, Jefferson militia colonel, and in 1783 one of Kentucky's first two judges. On April 8 that year he rode toward Bullitt's Lick in a scarlet coat; a shot from ambush dropped him, and he died two days later at 32.

name: Georgetown / Royal Spring
subtitle: Scott County / Elijah Craig spring
history: In July 1774 John Floyd claimed a thousand acres around a big Bluegrass spring. John McClelland built a cabin and stockade above it in 1775; an attack on December 29, 1776, killed McClelland, and the station emptied in 1777. Baptist preacher Elijah Craig later laid out Lebanon on the same spring, won a 1784 Virginia charter, and in 1790 renamed the place George Town for Washington. Scott County's seat still drinks from Royal Spring.

name: Leestown
subtitle: Franklin County / Kentucky River port
history: In 1773 the McAfee company and Hancock Taylor surveyed a buffalo crossing on the Kentucky River about a mile north of today’s Frankfort. Hancock and Willis Lee planted a village on the north bank in 1775, the first Anglo-American settlement north of the river. Raids emptied it in 1777; it returned as a tobacco warehouse and shipping port for hemp, corn, and whiskey, and in 1827 limestone for the Old State House was quarried from the riverbank here.

name: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
subtitle: Shelby & Jefferson counties / 1781 massacre
history: Daniel's younger brother Squire Boone carved his name into a Clear Creek rock, painted the letters red, and by spring 1780 planted Shelby County's first large station about two miles north of present Shelbyville. After an April 1781 wound left Squire's right arm permanently short, most settlers fled toward Linn's Station and walked into the Long Run Massacre of September 13. He later rebuilt a mill on the burnt site before land debts cost him the station.

name: Paris Founding
subtitle: Bourbon County seat / 1789–1790
history: Joseph Houston's 1776 station sat near Doyle Spring. Lawrence Protzman later platted 250 acres and in 1789 got Virginia to charter the town as Hopewell as Bourbon County's seat. In 1790 James Garrard and locals renamed it Paris to match the county, itself named for France's Bourbon kings who backed the Revolution. The post office briefly ran as Bourbonton before Paris stuck.

name: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
subtitle: Warren County / hunting-ground conflict
history: Shawnee held the larger northern and central Kentucky hunting grounds; Cherokee worked closer to Cumberland Gap. When long hunters stacked pelts for eastern markets, Native parties treated them as poachers. Around late 1769 a Shawnee band with Captain Will Emery took Boone and John Stewart’s six-month haul and warned them home: stay out, or the wasps and yellowjackets would sting. Not blank wilderness—a contested commons.

name: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
subtitle: Fayette County / 1750–51 survey
history: Fifteen-plus years before Boone’s fame, the Ohio Company hired surveyor Christopher Gist to probe the Ohio Valley down toward the Falls. Crossing into Kentucky from the Scioto mouth, his journal logged rich bottomlands, canebrakes, buffalo plains, and Native towns. Shawnee at Lower Shawneetown warned him off the Falls; he brought the company a fossil “beest” tooth from Big Bone country and the first detailed English read of northeastern Kentucky.

name: Jacob Spears
subtitle: Bourbon County / early bourbon whiskey
history: Pennsylvania-born Revolutionary veteran Jacob Spears settled near Paris in Bourbon County and was distilling by the 1790s. Thomas Metcalfe built his stone house (“Stone Castle”) around 1790; the farm still holds a springhouse and whiskey storehouse—Kentucky’s most complete early distiller’s complex. Spears floated barrels down the Licking to the Ohio and on to New Orleans, and he is often credited among the first to market the county’s whiskey under the name that stuck: bourbon.

name: John Filson
subtitle: Jefferson County / Filson Club pin
history: Pennsylvania schoolteacher and surveyor John Filson reached Lexington around 1783 with land warrants for more than 12,000 acres. In 1784 he published The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke—the first written history of the country—with a companion map engraved in Philadelphia. The book’s appendix carried the earliest printed Boone narrative; in 1788 Filson helped plat Losantiville (later Cincinnati) and that October vanished while surveying near the Great Miami.

name: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
subtitle: Franklin County / first KY railroad
history: On January 27, 1830, Kentucky chartered the Lexington & Ohio—the commonwealth’s first railroad, and among the first west of the Alleghenies—to tie Lexington to the Ohio River. Track used English strap iron spiked to quarried limestone sills; horses pulled early cars, then steam. The “Daniel Boone” engine made Lexington to Frankfort in about two and a half hours in 1835, cracking open Bluegrass freight toward the river long before the Civil War.

name: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
subtitle: Shelby County / Tick Creek
history: Born Spotsylvania County, Va., October 16, 1761, Bland Williams Ballard came to Kentucky in 1779 and scouted for George Rogers Clark. With Robert Tyler he helped plant Tyler Station on Tick Creek east of Shelbyville around 1781. In 1788 Delaware warriors killed his father and several siblings near the station; Ballard fought through Fallen Timbers, survived capture at Frenchtown, represented Shelby County in the General Assembly, and died September 5, 1853. Ballard County carries his name.

name: Gaitskill Mound
subtitle: Montgomery County / Adena tablets
history: On Mount Sterling’s northern bypass, Gaitskill Mound is an Adena earthwork (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 700) listed on the National Register in 1975. Unlike many looted mounds, it yielded rare engraved stone and clay tablets recovered through University of Kentucky work associated with W.S. Webb—ritual objects tied to Adena cremation and mound ceremony rather than everyday trash. The site anchors Montgomery County’s deep Woodland past beneath the later townscape.

name: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
subtitle: Woodford County / Labrot & Graham ground
history: Scottish physician-chemist James C. Crow began advising Oscar Pepper's Woodford County farm still on Glenn's Creek by 1833. After Pepper rebuilt in stone (1837–38), Crow returned as master distiller (1840–55), measuring mash temperatures, yeast, and acidity with scientific care that fixed sour-mash practice as commercial habit. His whiskey shipped far beyond Kentucky; Old Crow later took his name, and the limestone valley still hosts Woodford Reserve on the old Pepper ground.

name: Isaac Shelby
subtitle: Lincoln County / Traveler's Rest
history: Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant, then helped lead the Overmountain Men to victory at Kings Mountain in 1780. He moved to Kentucky in the 1780s, helped push statehood, and in 1792 became the commonwealth's first governor; sixteen years later he returned as fifth governor and led militia at the Battle of the Thames. Shelby County still carries his name, and Traveler's Rest marks his home ground.

name: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill
subtitle: Lincoln County / Crab Orchard
history: Near Crab Orchard, William Whitley finished Sportsman's Hill (1787–1794), often called Kentucky's first brick house—thick walls, elevated windows, and hiding places against raids. Beside it he ran a clay oval where horses raced counter-clockwise, a pointed break from English turf clockwise. The house and hill remain a Lincoln County historic site.

name: Estill's Defeat
subtitle: Montgomery County / Little Mountain 1782
history: On March 22, 1782, Capt. James Estill and about 25 Lincoln County militiamen overtook a Wyandot raiding party at Little Mountain Creek, near today’s Mount Sterling. After nearly two hours of fighting, Lt. William Miller’s left flank broke, the Wyandots closed, and Estill was killed in hand-to-hand combat along with six of his men. The fight—also called the Battle of Little Mountain—was one of the bloodiest single engagements of Kentucky’s “Year of Blood.”

name: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
subtitle: Bell County / geologic doorway
history: In March 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker led a Loyal Land Company party through the Appalachians and on April 13 recorded Cave Gap: a plain Indian road, a spring pouring from a cave, marked trees, and a pass visible for miles. He named the gap and nearby river for the Duke of Cumberland and later had a small cabin raised near present Barbourville—the first Euro-American house claimed in Kentucky. Walker’s journal mapped the geologic doorway later generations would pour through.
marker_title: Lewis and Clark in Kentucky - Cumberland Gap

name: Catherine Spears Carpenter
subtitle: Casey County / 1818 sour-mash recipes
history: Twice-widowed Catherine Spears Carpenter ran a large Casey County farm after 1806, raising crops, livestock, and surplus corn into whiskey. County tax records show her paying on 100 gallons of spirits in 1815. An 1818 manuscript in the Carpenter Family Papers preserves sweet-mash and sour-mash distilling recipes she used to instruct her household—one of the earliest written American sour-mash records, decades before James Crow’s fame.

name: Wickliffe Mounds
subtitle: Ballard County / Mississippian town
history: Mississippian farmers founded Wickliffe around AD 1100 on a bluff over the Ohio, three miles from the Mississippi confluence. They built platform mounds, a plaza, houses, and after 1175 a cemetery mound; by 1350 the community capped its mounds and left. In the 1930s a promoter opened graves to tourists as “Ancient Buried City”; Murray State later professionalized the research, and the site became a state historic site in 2004.

name: Falls of the Ohio
subtitle: Clarksville / Jefferson fossil beds
history: About 390 million years ago a shallow Devonian sea laid down the Jeffersonville Limestone—coral banks and stromatoporoid sponges now exposed at the Falls of the Ohio. Those hard shelves made the only major rapids on the river, so flatboats had to portage; Louisville and the Indiana towns grew at that choke point. George Rogers Clark staged from Corn Island in 1778. The beds have been a National Natural Landmark since 1966.

name: Lower Shawneetown
subtitle: Greenup County / Scioto mouth KY bank
history: Long before stations dotted the Bluegrass, a major Shawnee town straddled the Ohio at the Scioto’s mouth near today’s South Portsmouth. English maps called it Lower Shawneetown; by 1751 eyewitnesses put the population around 1,200. It was a diplomatic hub and western end of Pennsylvania’s southern deerskin trade until 1758, when the Shawnee moved north. Kentucky archaeology still holds Fort Ancient pottery mixed with mid-1700s trade goods from the Bentley and related sites on the Kentucky bank.

name: Indian Knoll
subtitle: Late Archaic shell midden · Ohio County
history: Five thousand years before the first stations, Late Archaic hunter-gatherers kept returning to a shell midden on the Green River in Ohio County. Indian Knoll (15OH2) yielded over a thousand burials, twenty-three dog burials, and more than 50,000 artifacts when University of Kentucky crews dug it in the late 1930s WPA years. In the early 1990s it and nineteen other Green River shell middens became National Historic Landmarks.

name: Danville Constitution Square
subtitle: Boyle County / statehood conventions
history: After the Kentucky District court moved from Harrodsburg to Crow’s Station, Danville’s public square (laid out 1785) hosted ten conventions from 1784 to 1792. Delegates there framed the first state constitution in April 1792, clearing the way for Kentucky to enter the Union as the fifteenth state on June 1. Replicas of the log courthouse, jail, and meetinghouse still mark the ground.

name: Mount Horeb Adena / Adena Park
subtitle: Fayette County / UK Adena Park
history: Above Elkhorn Creek near Lexington, Adena people built a circular ditch-and-embankment enclosure more than 2,000 years ago for periodic ritual gatherings. WPA digs under William S. Webb in 1939 found a ring of large paired posts that likely screened ceremonies before the earthen walls went up. The University of Kentucky now protects a partially reconstructed site as Adena Park.

name: Fox Farm Fort Ancient
subtitle: Mason County / 15Ms1
history: On a broad ridgetop near Mays Lick, Fort Ancient farmers lived at Fox Farm (15Ms1) from about 1300 into the mid-1600s—one of the longest-lived villages of its kind in the Ohio Valley. Houses first ringed a plaza, then clustered around a large public building as population grew. Residents planted corn, beans, and squash, managed turkey harvests, and once curated eleven deer jaws as a ritual offering inside a house wall.

name: Indian Fort Mountain
subtitle: Madison County / Berea Pinnacles
history: On a knobby ridge south of Berea, dry-laid stone walls ring Indian Fort Mountain (15Ma25) in the Berea College Forest. Hopewell-era Middle Woodland people built them about 2,000 years ago as a hilltop enclosure, more a ceremonial marker than a stockade. Tests in 1980 treated the tumbled rock as linear mounds rather than a fighting wall. The site went on the National Register in 1983; hikers still climb the Pinnacles over the same ground.

name: Ashland Central Park Adena Mounds
subtitle: Boyd County / Central Park
history: Six conical Adena burial mounds still sit in Ashland’s Central Park, roughly 15–20 feet across and 4–6 feet high in a slight curve. UK archaeologists Webb and Funkhouser recorded them in 1932; a 1930s survey said no Kentucky city held more prehistoric evidence than Ashland, though many other local mounds were leveled for streets. Listed on the National Register in 1974, they mark Woodland mound-builder presence along the Ohio centuries before historic tribes.

name: Mount Sterling Founding
subtitle: Montgomery County seat / Little Mountain
history: Explorers out of Boonesborough called a tree-covered Adena burial mound “the Little Mountain.” Scotsman Hugh Forbes began selling lots beside it around 1790; in 1792 the Kentucky Assembly chartered the town on 640 acres. Forbes meant Mount Stirling (for Stirling, Scotland, plus the mound); the misspelled “Sterling” stuck. The mound—once about 25 feet high at Queen and Locust—was leveled in 1845, and Mount Sterling became Montgomery County’s seat.

name: Carlston Annis Shell Mound
subtitle: Butler County / 15Bt5
history: On the Green River floodplain in Butler County, Carlston Annis (15Bt5) is a Late Archaic shell midden about 300 by 350 feet and more than six feet thick, piled up beside a mussel shoal between roughly 3000 and 1000 BC. WPA crews under William S. Webb dug nearly half an acre in 1940–41; later work by the Shell Mound Archaeological Project refined the picture of repeated seasonal camps with burials, dog burials, hearths, and pestle caches.

name: Winchester Founding
subtitle: Clark County seat
history: Clark County was carved from Fayette and Bourbon on December 6, 1792, and named for George Rogers Clark. Justices first met at John Strode’s station, then voted to put the public buildings on John Baker’s land by his spring. On December 17, 1793, the Assembly established a town there named Winchester, after Baker’s hometown in Frederick County, Virginia. A two-room log courthouse went up in 1794; Winchester remains Clark’s seat.

name: Hardin Village Fort Ancient
subtitle: Greenup County / 15Gp22
history: On the Ohio floodplain in Greenup County near South Shore, Hardin Village was a late Fort Ancient town occupied from the late 1500s into the early 1600s and covering more than ten acres. University of Kentucky digs in 1939 and again in the 2010s mapped large bark-walled houses, storage pits, and family cemeteries. Triangular endscrapers point to intensive hide work for long-distance exchange—marine shell and brass among the imports—just as the protohistoric Ohio Valley was tipping toward abandonment.

name: Richmond Founding
subtitle: Madison County / Miller's barn courthouse
history: Madison County's first seat sat at hillside Milford with thin water. In 1798 the legislature let the court move onto Revolutionary War veteran Col. John Miller's land along Otter Creek; the county paid angry Milford residents before carting records to Miller's barn. On July 4, 1798, trustees named the new seat Richmond for Miller's Virginia birthplace, surveyed fifty acres into lots, and built a brick courthouse on the barn site in 1799. Richmond incorporated in 1809.

subtitle: Boone County · Adena burial mounds
history: Robbins Mounds (15Be3) is an Adena burial complex in Boone County excavated by WPA–UK crews in 1939, revealing circular screens and log tombs typical of Early Woodland ceremonial architecture along the Ohio.

name: Basil Hayden Sr. / Holy Cross (Pottinger's Creek)
subtitle: Nelson County / Pottinger's Creek
history: Basil Hayden Sr. led Maryland Catholic settlers to Pottinger's Creek in 1785; high-rye whiskey tradition and Holy Cross Church land mark early Nelson County bourbon and Catholic frontier settlement.

subtitle: Montgomery County · Adena mounds
history: Three conical Adena mounds (15Mm6–8) once crowned a Bluegrass ridgetop in Montgomery County. University of Kentucky crews excavated two in 1937 and found paired-post screens and log tombs typical of Adena mortuary practice. The mounds date to the Adena period (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 200), not the excavation year.

subtitle: McLean County · Late Archaic shell midden
history: On the Godfrey Ward farm along the Green River, the Ward Site (15McL11) is a Late Archaic shell-midden cemetery in the same Green River series as Indian Knoll and Carlston Annis. WPA crews dug about 16,000 square feet in 1938 and catalogued hundreds of burials; the occupation itself belongs to the Late Archaic (roughly 3000–1000 B.C.).

name: Read Shell Midden (15Bt10)
subtitle: Butler County · Late Archaic shell midden
history: On the Green River west of Morgantown, the Read Shell Midden (15Bt10) is a Late Archaic camp-and-cemetery in the same mussel-shoal world as Indian Knoll, Carlston Annis, and Ward. WPA crews dug it 1937–1939 under William S. Webb; more than 240 burials were identified. Occupation years are Late Archaic (~3000–1000 BC), not the dig dates. Approximate published coords (NRHP address restricted).

name: Stanford / St. Asaph (Logan’s Fort)
subtitle: Lincoln County · Standing Fort · county seat 1786
history: In spring 1775 Benjamin Logan and John Floyd’s survey party camped at Buffalo Spring and planted St. Asaph; Logan’s Fort rose there by early 1777 and never fell—nicknamed Standing Fort after the May 1777 siege. On May 16, 1786, the court seated permanently on Logan’s fifty-acre gift a mile east as Stanford, still Lincoln County’s seat.

name: Newt Kash Hollow (15Mf1)
subtitle: Menifee County · Early Woodland rockshelter
history: In Menifee County’s Red River country, Newt Kash rockshelter preserved Early Woodland plant beds—squash, sunflower, goosefoot, and sumpweed among the earliest clear domesticates from a Kentucky shelter, occupied intensively around 3,000 years ago. Later readings also treat the fiber, cradleboard, and medicinal plants as a possible women’s retreat and medicine place.

name: Col. John Todd of Lexington
subtitle: Fayette militia colonel · Blue Licks 1782 · Todd County
history: Pennsylvania-born lawyer John Todd (1750–1782) reached Kentucky around 1775, sat in Virginia’s legislature for Kentucky County, rode with George Rogers Clark to Kaskaskia and Vincennes, and was named civil commandant of Illinois County. He became Fayette’s first militia colonel and a Lexington trustee. After Bryan Station’s siege he led the pursuit that ended at Blue Licks on August 19, 1782, where he was killed at 32; Todd County (1819) still carries his name.

name: Muir Site (15Js86)
subtitle: Jessamine County · early Fort Ancient (Osborne phase)
history: West of Nicholasville on a Jessamine County ridge, Muir is an early Fort Ancient (Osborne phase) hamlet dated roughly A.D. 1000–1200. UK crews dug it in 1985 ahead of the Nicholasville Bypass and found only one to three small square-to-rectangular basin houses in use at a time—dispersed households rather than a later plaza village. Muir shows Bluegrass Fort Ancient life before the big nucleated towns.

name: Newport at the Licking Mouth
subtitle: Campbell County · charter 1795 · Newport Barracks 1803
history: Hubbard Taylor platted the Ohio–Licking point for the family; James Taylor Jr. settled in 1793, pushed Campbell County through in 1794, and on December 14, 1795 the General Assembly chartered Newport on Taylor land. He named it for Admiral Christopher Newport of Jamestown fame, reserved a public square and riverfront common, and in 1803 sold the army five acres at the Licking mouth for what became Newport Barracks.

name: Adams Site (15Fu4)
subtitle: Fulton County · Mississippian town on Bayou de Chien
history: Near Hickman in Fulton County, on Bayou de Chien toward the Mississippi, the Adams Site is a Mississippian town built over an earlier Late Woodland village. Platform mounds around a central plaza (plus a smaller plaza southwest), deep village middens, and occupation roughly 1100–1500 CE place it with sister border towns like Wickliffe and Sassafras Ridge.

name: Drennon Springs
subtitle: Henry County · salt lick & early boiling works
history: In Henry County, Jacob Drennon and Matthew Bracken claimed the big salt lick on July 26, 1773; Nicholas Cresswell in 1775 described some fifty acres of buffalo-trampled ground and springs strong enough to leave salt crusts in the sun. Virginia’s Patrick Henry patented 400 acres including the springs to George Rogers Clark in 1785, and boiling works rose that winter.

name: Maj. Joseph Bowman
subtitle: Clark’s second-in-command · Harrodsburg petition 1776 · died 1779
history: Virginia-born Joseph Bowman came to Kentucky by 1775, signed the 1776 Harrodsburg county petition, and in 1778 raised a company for George Rogers Clark. As Clark’s second-in-command he took Prairie du Rocher, St. Philippe, and Cahokia after Kaskaskia fell, kept a day-by-day journal of the flooded winter march to Vincennes, and was promoted major just as a celebratory powder explosion burned him badly. He died at Fort Patrick Henry on about August 14–15, 1779 — the only American officer lost in the Illinois campaign.

name: Owensboro / Yellow Banks
subtitle: William Smeathers cabin ~1797 · Owensborough 1817
history: Frontiersman William Smeathers built a cabin on the Ohio’s yellow clay banks about 1797–98; the landing was already called Yellow Banks. After Daviess County formed in 1815, the town was laid out in 1816 and chartered Owensborough in 1817 for Col. Abraham Owen.

name: Col. William Russell III
subtitle: Kings Mountain · Fayette 1783 · Russell County namesake
history: Born Culpeper County, Virginia, 1758; rode west on his father’s 1773 Kentucky attempt. Aide to Col. William Campbell at Kings Mountain; settled Fayette County in 1783 on military land. Early Kentucky house member, Northwest Indian War militia leader, and colonel of the 7th U.S. Infantry (Fort Harrison, Peoria War). Russell County is named for him.

name: Annis Mound & Village (15Bt2)
subtitle: Butler County · Middle Mississippian mound center
history: On the Green River’s Big Bend in Butler County, Annis (15Bt2 / 15Bt20) was a Middle Mississippian mound center occupied about 800–1300 CE, with expanding palisades and a large platform mound. Pinned from the 2026-09-17 KY History update (occupation years, not WPA/NRHP dates).

name: Cumberland Falls
subtitle: Rockcastle conglomerate · moonbow · gorge retreat
history: Where the Cumberland crosses hard Rockcastle conglomerate, softer rock below keeps a ~68-foot drop—the “Niagara of the South.” The falls retreated about 45 miles upstream cutting the gorge; clear full-moon nights bring a moonbow. Geology-focused pin (no modern park year).

name: Glasgow / Barren County seat
subtitle: John Gorin’s Big Spring · barrens · 1799
history: Barren County was authorized December 20, 1798, from Green and Warren, named for the open barrens prairie. In 1799 settlers chose John Gorin’s Big Spring for the county seat; Gorin opened a tavern that year and put land and cash toward public buildings on the pea-vine hill that became Glasgow’s square. The legislature recognized the town in 1809.

name: Maj. Silas Harlan / Harlan’s Station
subtitle: Salt River south of Harrodsburg · Blue Licks 1782
history: Virginia-born Major Silas Harlan (c. 1752–1782) came to Kentucky in 1774, built Harlan’s Station on the Salt River about seven miles south of Harrodsburg in 1778, and commanded spies in George Rogers Clark’s Illinois campaign. He fell leading an advance party at Blue Licks on August 19, 1782; Harlan County (1819) carries his name.

name: Chiggerville (15Oh1)
subtitle: Ohio County · Late Archaic Green River shell midden
history: On the Green River floodplain in Ohio County, the Late Archaic Chiggerville shell midden (roughly 3000–1000 BC) sits beside an old mussel shoal more than four feet thick. Digs recovered dense burials, hearths, mussels, fish, nuts, and Green River humped bannerstones—another node in Kentucky’s densest Archaic shell-midden landscape.

name: Salts Cave (15Ht4)
subtitle: Mammoth Cave NP · Early Woodland sulfate mining
history: Inside Mammoth Cave National Park, Salts Cave was one of several passages Early Woodland people used most intensively about 1000–200 BC. They mined wall sulfates—gypsum for pigment, mirabilite as medicine and seasoning—and carried cane torches, textile slippers, baskets, and gourd containers deep underground.

name: Capt. Jack Jouett / Craig’s Creek
subtitle: Midnight ride 1781 · Woodford house 1797
history: On the night of June 3–4, 1781, Virginia militia captain John “Jack” Jouett Jr. spotted Banastre Tarleton’s British cavalry near Cuckoo Tavern and rode about forty miles of backwoods trails to warn Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and the Virginia Assembly at Charlottesville. In 1782 he moved west, backed Kentucky statehood, served in the Kentucky House, and in 1797 built the brick house still standing on Craig’s Creek near Versailles.

name: Shepherdsville / Salt River falls
subtitle: Adam Shepherd · Bullitt County seat · 1793
history: On December 11, 1793, the Kentucky General Assembly established a town on fifty acres of Adam Shepherd’s land on the north side of Salt River, at the falls where the great road to Bullitt’s Lick crossed. When Bullitt County was organized in 1796–97, Shepherdsville became the seat, anchoring settlement between the Wilderness Road corridor and the Falls of the Ohio salt trade.

name: Capt. Nathaniel Hart / White Oak Springs
subtitle: Hart’s Station · Madison County · 1779–1782
history: Capt. Nathaniel Hart (1734–1782), a Transylvania Company proprietor and chief negotiator with the Cherokee, came to Boonesborough in 1775 and in 1779 settled White Oak Springs (Hart’s Station) about a mile from the fort, joined by Dutch families from Pennsylvania. He was killed nearby in 1782; his daughter Susannah later married Isaac Shelby, Kentucky’s first and fifth governor.

name: Henderson / Red Banks
subtitle: Hopkins–Allin plan · April 6, 1797
history: The Ohio River bluff known as Red Banks sat on the Virginia grant later confirmed to Richard Henderson & Company. On April 6, 1797, Gen. Samuel Hopkins and surveyor Thomas Allin finished laying out the town of Henderson—named for the company founder, who had died in 1785. That plan is still treated as the city’s birthday; Henderson County followed in 1798–99.

name: Turk Site (15Ce6)
subtitle: Carlisle County · Mississippian Dorena–Medley
history: On a bluff spur near Bardwell overlooking the Mississippi floodplain, the Turk Site (15Ce6) was a small Mississippian regional center of about 2.5 hectares. Occupied mainly in the Dorena phase (about 1100–1300 CE) and into the Medley phase, it arranged platform mounds around a plaza—tightened by the spur’s narrow geography.

name: Lost River Cave
subtitle: Bowling Green · Pennyroyal karst · late-1700s mill
history: Under Bowling Green, Lost River Cave is a Pennyroyal karst system cut in Mississippian St. Louis and Ste. Genevieve limestones: a surface stream sinks into roughly seven miles of passages. Settlers harnessed the flow for a grist mill at the cave mouth by the late 1700s; today the preserve offers Kentucky’s only underground boat tour.

name: Hansen Site (15GP14)
subtitle: Greenup County · Scioto mouth terrace
history: Near South Portsmouth in Greenup County, the Hansen Site sits on an Ohio River terrace just upstream from Lower Shawneetown and across from the Scioto mouth. Excavations document Late Archaic summer camps around 2000 BCE, then denser Middle–Late Woodland communities (about 300–600 CE); Fort Ancient people used the terrace later.

name: Natural Bridge
subtitle: Corbin Sandstone arch · Powell–Wolfe · state park 1926
history: In Powell and Wolfe counties, a 78-foot-long, 65-foot-high arch of Corbin Sandstone (Breathitt Formation, Middle Pennsylvanian) spans a gorge on the Middle Fork of the Red River. Long a landmark for Indigenous hunters and settlers, the site became a railroad excursion stop in the 1890s and one of Kentucky’s original state parks in 1926.

name: David Snowden homeplace
subtitle: Lee County · St. Helens · Middle Fork Kentucky River
history: Historic Snowden homeplace near St. Helens (Lee County), on a knob by the Middle Fork Kentucky River (KY 52 east of Beattyville). David Snowden Sr. (1759 near Perth Amboy, N.J. – 1839 Estill Co.) served as a Revolutionary War frontier “Indian spy” and guard from Washington Co., Pa. (federal pension W9308), and also on Gen. Lachlan McIntosh’s 1778 Ohio campaign and Col. William Crawford’s 1782 Sandusky expedition; he married Nancy Hazelrigg in 1782. His son David Snowden Jr. (1786–1852) built a log cabin, kitchen, and quarters here about 1825; a later two-story clapboard house on sandstone had a wing that served as the St. Helens post office. The family also appears in Owsley County around 1850 before Lee County split. The abandoned house was photographed extensively and was reportedly demolished after a fire. Photos: https://abandonedonline.net/location/david-snowden-house/ and https://abandonedonline.net/david-snowden-jrs-house/ . Pension abstract: https://kygenweb.net/estill/military/revwar/snowden01.htm.

name: Ann McGinty
subtitle: First spinning wheel over Cumberland Gap · Harrodstown · d. 1815
history: Anne Kennedy (later Poage, Lindsay, and McGinty) crossed into Kentucky in September 1775 with a spinning wheel—the first brought over Cumberland Gap—and soon helped her husband William Poage build looms at Harrodstown. Their linsey-woolsey cloth became a frontier staple; she later ran an ordinary (tavern-inn) and is buried in the Fort Harrod Pioneer Cemetery (d. 1815).

name: Henry McKenna
subtitle: Fairfield · Nelson County · Old Line sour mash 1855–1883
history: Irish immigrant Henry McKenna of County Derry settled at Fairfield in Nelson County, began distilling in a mill shed by 1855 (under a barrel a day), and built a brick distillery by 1883. He sold only "H. McKenna Old Line" sour mash—never green whisky under three years—and stamped barrels with an Irish harp. The brand later survived Prohibition as medicinal whisky; Heaven Hill revived it in the modern era.

name: Estill Springs
subtitle: Estill County · Irvine · KY 89 (marker 555)
history: Mineral springs about half a mile north of Irvine on today’s KY 89, long known to Shawnee camps and early Kentucky explorers (Boone, Boyle, McAfee, and others). Operated as a resort from 1814 until the hotel burned in 1924; white sulphur water, Sweet Lick Knob views, and a popular ballroom drew visitors from across the state. In 1861 owner Col. Sidney M. Barnes organized the 8th Kentucky Infantry (USA) here; the grounds later hosted Confederate reunions of Morgan’s men, including the last. Kentucky Historical Society marker #555 stands on Main Street across from Estill Springs Elementary. Historic photo (c. 1910): https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/sprague_photo_collection/117/

Map pin uses Irvine town center (Nominatim) because the exact mill footprint is not documented in the catalog record; treat as a place-level pin for the historic sawmill operation, not a surveyed building outline.
